fixed.author: Samuel Aniensis
fixed.before: 8. The son of Ara, born of Ara, was Anushavan. For then, since my body was entirely immature, neither my eyes nor my tongue nor my heart cooperated with one another toward the learning of instruction. For it is not possible for one who is still childish in mind to be taught knowledge easily, since every child, taking pleasure in games and idleness, does not set his mind attentively on instruction. And I too, O king, being in the same way at that time in both age and understanding, could gain no fruit at all from what I was taught, since I did not fix my mind on these things at all, but, being childish, kept it scattered. But my teacher Syntipas, observing the youthfulness of my age, did not teach me heavily, nor did he use difficult words with me at the beginning, so that I should not be worn down from the start by the weight of difficult and hard-to-grasp things and cast out of my mind everything I was taught — for my teacher knew that if he taught me immoderately from the beginning, I could easily have rebelled against him and left him, since I am a king's son — but by shaping me little by little with his words he thus skilfully led me up to the perfection of philosophy. And I, laying hold of a more mature understanding, kept in my heart all the things taught me by him, and gathering together my formerly scattered reason, straining my ears to listening and my tongue to the practice and weaving of words, and (having learned) to apply my hands to punctuating, I thus in the space of only six months grasped most exactly everything taught me, and came to share in all philosophy and understanding, the divine power surely also helping both me and the zeal of the one who initiated me.' The king, greatly delighted in heart at these words of the boy, sent up words of thanksgiving to God, and kept extolling to the utmost the boy's understanding and philosophy, and acknowledged his thanks to Syntipas. Then he orders that wicked woman, who had plotted to destroy his son, to be brought before him; and when she stood there, the king says to her: 'Reveal to me, woman, holding nothing back out of fear, why you were eager to destroy my son, and what the manner of this mischief of yours was.' The woman replied and said: 'You know, most mighty king, that nothing is dearer to any man than his own life. For even if someone lives in poverty or is oppressed by some misfortune of life, he nonetheless still clings to his own life. Now, I took your boy to myself at your command for this reason: that, out of service to your majesty, I might find out from him in private by what cause he was restrained from speaking. And I kept coaxing him with all sorts of questions and flatteries, and softening the hardness of his silence with gentle words, until I induced him to answer me one word. This he uttered angrily and sharply, and said to me: "I will answer you nothing for now, woman, until seven days from now have passed. Then I will give you the answer you deserve." I, greatly alarmed at this word and becoming very frightened, and suspecting that I would be exposed to danger from the boy, saw how to escape by contrivance the ruin [coming] from him. And thereupon, impelled by satanic working, I lied against your son and treacherously accused him before your majesty. I know my sin and confess it openly, denying nothing of it. But you, most great king, do with me what seems good to you, as your God-guided majesty may please.' The king, looking at his grandees who stood by, says to them: 'What counsel do you give my majesty about this matter, and of what punishment would this woman be worthy?' One of the grandees replied and says to the king: 'It is just, O king, that her hands and feet be cut off.' Another says: 'Justice does not seem so good to me; rather, it is fitting that her heart be dug out while she is alive.' And another of them again said in reply that her tongue should be cut out. The woman, hearing such verdicts and what punishments they were proposing to the king for her, spoke a fable of this sort to them, saying: 'What you declare against me, grandees, is like the example of a certain fox, who used to enter a certain city by night. Her way in was through the window of the little house of a certain leather-worker. And whenever she entered his house through it, she ate up his hides. Then that leather-worker, seeing the tears that had been made in his hides, at once sets a very strong trap for her. The fox afterwards, entering again through that window as was her habit, is at once caught in the trap. But the fox, being wicked and wily, escaped the trap that held her by some well-devised contrivance. And she went round the whole city to find some other window through which she could get out of the city; but it was walled in on every side. And though she toiled the whole night, she could find no way out at all; and as the day was dawning, she reasoned with herself and said: "If day comes on, I shall be seen by the dogs, and they will not leave me alone until they have divided my flesh among them. But I know what I must do." And having said this she goes to the gate of the city, and stretching herself out near the doorpost on the inside, she pretended to be dead and breathless. She used this device waiting for the city gate to be opened, so that she might at once make her escape through it in a rush and be rid of the danger she feared. When she was thus stretched out as if dead, and the gate had been opened toward dawn, someone saw her and said to himself: "Truly the tail of this fox is very useful as a ready sponge for a mill workshop." Saying this, he at once drew his knife and cut it off. The fox, her tail cut off, bore it bravely in silence. Then another man passing by and seeing her spoke thus: "I have heard that if one of the infants goes on crying for a long time, there is nothing else for curing him and stopping his crying like a fox's ears. If these were brought [away] from this child, his crying would not go on long." And having said this he cut off that fox's ears with a knife. And the fox bore this too bravely, (so that) by the (appearance) of being dead she might escape death. Another man passing through there said to the others: "I too, men, have heard that if someone has pain and suffering in his teeth, he should pull out a fox's tooth and put it on the suffering tooth, and at once he will obtain a cure of the affliction." So that man too, having said this, at once took up a stone and smashed all the fox's teeth; and she bravely endured this punishment too. And thus she went on enduring the pains, until another man passing by said: "I too have heard that the fox's heart serves as a pain-relieving drug, and that it is healing for all diseases." At that very hour it happened that the city gate was opened; and at once the fox leapt out and ran off through the gate at great speed and escaped the danger hanging over her. And I too now, wretched as I am, O king, am ready to endure all the other things that the grandees of your majesty have advised your majesty, but to bear having my heart dug out I cannot. For it is the cause of a violent death.'

objection.original: Quid mirum si te Deus et generosos liberos, propriamque 118 familiam
objection.english: What wonder if God permits you and your noble children and your own household
objection.explain: The children and household belong to God, the father in the comparison, not to the addressee: 'you and his noble children, his own household'.

fixed.author: Maximus Taurinensis Episcopus
fixed.before: CHAPTER VII. — Therefore, while we first endure small and moderate things, it is necessary that we learn to bear greater or the greatest. For it is the bright mark of our warfare to set one's step through steep places, to be carried through hard things, and to bear the hard censure of miseries with hard strength. Our way to heaven lies through rough places, through narrow places, through hard windings and [rugged] places; and that way he has not held who was unwilling to be tried. To heaven God calls the bravest soldier, whom afflictions escort with glories accompanying, and rewards receive as a victor about to reign. Does he meanwhile lay on us anything sheer, which exceeds the measure of a balanced weight? Does he impose what by excess goes beyond the capacity of our virtue? The most faithful governor orders the burden to be laid on according to strength. This the proclamation of Paul attests and proves: God is faithful, he says, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear (1 Cor. 10). Let us believe that we are so driven and ruled by the Lord as pupils are ruled by teachers of schools: they impose and lay the most labour on those whom they see to excel the rest in clever talents; and we too adjust the burden for the animals subject to our dominion according to the measure of their strength: we lay strong loads on the stronger and small ones on the slender, so that use, that nourisher of virtue, may raise and advance their strength into the greatest robustness of youth. In this way our first lessons are beaten with light blows, so that thereafter they may prepare strength, made accustomed, for heavier ones, namely out of love of divine virtue. Although this reasoning abounds in many divine proofs, yet let us use some example also from worldly things; for it does no harm to use what belongs to others in that part in which it is ours. Do you suppose that their own children were hateful to the Spartans, whose natures and tender limbs, still ignorant of toil, they test, and, when public floggings are applied, paternal love itself exhorts them to bear the strokes of the whips bravely; and, when they are torn and half-dead, they entreat and beg them to persevere in setting wounds upon wounds? What wonder if God permits you and your noble children and your own household to be hard tried for the brightness of nourishing virtue, intending to confer everlasting kingdoms on the victors? He thus promises the prizes of toil against all evils whatever, and says: Whoever perseveres to the end, he will be saved (Matt. 10). And again: Come to me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11). A little of perishing time is the price of eternity. The devotion of tribulation will be repaid made fruitful with everlasting fruits. With us the kingdom is sought by a fruitful captivity; security is bought by dangers, rest is procured by sweat: For virtue, says the Apostle, is made perfect in infirmity (2 Cor. 12). It is certainly better to be shaken in the flesh by languid conditions than, with healthy limbs, to carry a conscience troubled by a blind punishment. For many fall sick with sins from the very idleness of the limbs. For while they are free from infirmities, the body must flow with a morbid slackness, and be dissolved by a deadly disease, and lead the man, wickedly healthy, headlong through vices and forests of errors...

objection.original: His iter est, quod comes libido periculis dictaverit peritura.
objection.english: Their road is the one which lust, their companion, dictates through dangers, [a road] destined to perish.
objection.explain: Peritura agrees with feminine libido, not neuter iter: lust, their companion, is destined to perish, not the road.

fixed.author: Maximus Taurinensis Episcopus
fixed.before: CHAPTER VIII. — Do you judge those free, or strangers to diseases, whom barbarous pleasures have bound? They have no chain, but luxury holds them in bonds with a deadly bite. They have fallen into the snares of deadly pleasures like birds captured by the fowler's trick, which, the more they try to escape, the more they entangle themselves in countless knots and sink into deeper folds. Are those really healthy whom an insane disease wraps up and tosses about? Truly sound is he whom God corrects with any lash whatever, who by chastising shows himself a lover of man: Those whom I love, says the Lord, I rebuke and chastise (Rev. 3). And therefore let him not judge himself healthy who lacks either diseases or squalor, and is not strengthened by the remedy of infirmity. Those indeed are wretched who grow torpid in the sluggish tranquillity of excessive happiness; whom a counterfeit health flatters, to deceive and cheat them; whom, namely, an eternal sickness will hold, which will afterwards torment the whole man with an eternal torturer. Their ways are as many as the pleasures that come to their aid. Their road is the one which lust, their companion, dictates through dangers, [a road] destined to perish. For seized by the windings of dragging vices, the wretched are rolled with various falls into destruction, on a most uncertain way, never to return; they stretch the mind toward outward things, after the manner of streams, which never flow back to their own source. Indeed they lead this life, whose companion is its end, with prosperous courses, as they themselves suppose; but the step at the last ends altogether badly, while at the very end one stands hard. And what does it profit to have run prosperously through dangers, if after the course it befalls one to perish? In vain, indeed, does a ship run into harbour through a proud and raging sea, with friendly waves and favourable prosperity, if it arrives with shipwreck, and the harbour receives it to perish. It is better, therefore, to arrive at the harbour of glory under the leading of any affliction whatever, than, after completing the course of morbid slackness in a delicate ship, to go out into punishments. Often, then, poverty is better than riches, deformity than beauty, insult than praises, servitude than power, weakness than strength, captivity than liberty, lowliness than rank. David, the illustrious prophet, expressed a song of this kind: It is good for me, Lord, he says, that you have humbled me, that I may learn your justifications (Ps. 118). Therefore it is better to be humbled by the losses of discipline by [God's] judgement than to be condemned with the world, as the Apostle says: When we are judged by the Lord, we are corrected, so that we may not be condemned with this world (1 Cor. 11). Therefore what is bestowed for our benefit out of the Lord's love, let us bear without murmuring. For discipline is applied by the Lord as a remedy by a physician. It belongs to the art of medicine sometimes to work with fire and iron. What wonder if the Lord, the physician of our souls, shakes us with whirlwinds, tests us with diseases, purges us with calamities? It belongs to our fortitude to be purged as if through fires and flames, in the manner of vessels, which divine Scripture attests and proves: The furnace, it says, proves the potter's vessels, and the trial of tribulation just men (Ecclus. 27). And elsewhere it says: Gold, and silver, and iron, and lead, and everything that has passed through fire, will be cleansed (Num. 31). Vessels never say to the potter: Why do you test us by the judgement of the flames, and burn and prove us with cooking fires? Unless the fire as judge pronounces them most fit by its judgement, they cannot be in use. We too, unless the judgement or testing of temptations has purged us, are found useless to the potter of our members, who burns us to cure us, tries us to free us, harasses us to save us. For nothing is so defiled, so filthy, that it is not cleansed of vices by purgings. Often, indeed, we have seen those soiled by reproach come into brightness, and iron covered with rust shine again with its former face. We have seen gold and silver purged by the discipline of the flame, and pruned trees revive with most joyful cultivation and be adorned with lovely shoots. We have seen barren things recalled to fruitfulness, and, the trunk being exhausted, the root accompanied by a very great crop. So too in us, whatever perhaps was seething under the pressure of sins, whatever stain of squalid old age stood in the way, has been shut out by the light of sickness. And therefore, brother, the sickness of your limbs, acting as a physician, has rendered you healthy. In you only the matter of the flesh lacks the health of strength; and lest it perhaps should trouble you, it is troubled by a useful disease. This is what the dog-star of old age strikes in all men, and, like hay, it withers, about to lose its own flower, as it is written: All flesh is hay, and all its glory like the flower of hay. The hay has withered, and the flower has fallen; but the word of the Lord remains for ever (Isa. 40). Let us therefore bear with equanimity if the body, which we read will perish like hay with its flowers falling, is tossed about exhausted by harmful evils, the body whose health has been wont to bring disease upon the soul, and to draw out deadly and barbarous pleasures against spiritual benefits. Often, indeed, the unbridled flesh has ungirded the soldiers of chastity. It is for our good, then, if we are chastised with long and biting scourges, [the flesh] by which nevertheless our chastity is assailed. Foolishly we love the flesh: we do not grieve over the prison and tomb of the soul. Therefore, scorning the fragility of the flesh itself, let us seize as a treasure, with the embraces of devotion, whatever befalls. It is timid for a Christian soldier to wish to remain in calm, after the manner of those who make merry. It belongs to a downcast mind to dread the whirlwind, but to an opposing one not to tremble amid opposing things. It belongs to unhappiness not to know adversity, to happiness to know how to engage with adversities, and to know how to fight. For since all the blows by which we are shaken, as we have already said, are born from a divine gift, let him know himself a stranger to the love of God who does not know how to be harassed by temptations, since the trumpet of the law impresses on our hearing with manifold song and says: The Lord your God tests you, it says, to know whether you love him with all your heart and with all your soul (Deut. 13). And elsewhere: Son, it says, do not neglect his discipline, and do not faint when you are corrected by him. For whom God loves he corrects (Prov. 3). And again: Do not despise the correction of the Lord, it says. For he himself gives pain, and he himself refreshments; he strikes, and his hands bestow health (Job 5).

Vessels never say to the potter: Why do you test us by the judgement of the flames, and burn and prove us with cooking fires? Unless the fire as judge pronounces them most fit by its judgement, they cannot be in use. fixed.author: Paschasius Diaconus
fixed.before: We read of the abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit: But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan. Who, then, except one who was of the same fullness, could fill him who fills all things? Of the apostles the divine word reports: And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with confidence. And a little later: How he is said to fill even whole nations, and yet is recognised to remain inexhaustible and full in himself. If the Spirit is created, of what angel or archangel has it ever been read that, received inwardly, he poured himself into any soul? Tell me, if you have ever read of any power and might among creatures that fills and possesses many things at once and, what is more, remains undiminished and [un]divided. It is impossible that a spiritual and rational creature should ever be able to be poured into a nature kindred to itself. So too a material thing cannot penetrate a material substance. God alone, in whom the Holy Spirit also is understood, simple, subtle, pure, glides into his handiwork, whether angelic or human, by the power of incorporeal divinity, which alone penetrates its own work and enters the hidden places of the human heart. But no heavenly creature can so far pour itself into or fill a man as to be able to know the hidden things of human thought. And therefore we read of God alone: You who alone know the hearts of men (Prov. 6). And again: For it knows how to discern hidden things. And if this is proper to divinity, how much more is it a mark of majesty to search the depths of the most high God in the person of the Holy Spirit. This privilege is owed to the Author alone, that he can enter the secret conscience. A soul can be joined to a soul, or an angel to an angel, but cannot be poured into it, because creatures of this kind are capable only of the Holy Spirit, that is, of God alone; because they are the vessels of their potter, they can be filled only by him by whom they were made from nothing, and without whom they are felt to be empty. So the substance of the soul, being corporeal matter, cannot at all be poured into another rational creature. For compared with the grossness of the outer man the soul can be called incorporeal, but referred to its author, to whom its matter is comprehensible and his handiwork palpable, by whom it can be enclosed and bound within a body and consigned to everlasting fire, as we read: that they may go into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels; to this author it is undoubtedly something corporeal. But perhaps you say: It is plain that even the troublesome violence of demons frequently pours itself into men whom it has received to tempt. It is not so: for they can enter the recesses of the body, but cannot reach the inner parts of the soul. It must be known, then, that the deceitful subtlety of spiritual wickedness disturbs by its onset those parts of the limbs which are at times wearied by too much wine or by the heat of fever. Thus hostile temptation knows how to creep into the senses of the soul through malice, but cannot flow into the recesses of the soul by nature. And therefore human minds and breasts take in such unclean spirits not by an infusion of natures, but conceive them by depravity of will. It is plain, therefore, that they cannot penetrate the substances of souls whose consciences they cannot know. For observation of the powers is common [to all], but that upon symptoms is peculiar to them. For one must either do away with it altogether as impossible, or grant that it is possible, but show that without reason it is impossible. First, then, that observation is impossible without reason, one might show by the following. The Empiricists concede that they do not make their observation upon all apparent symptoms. For they say they do not observe upon, say, fairness or whiteness, or a snub or a hooked nose. And yet they do observe a certain difference in colours, as with jaundiced patients, and in shape, as with fractures and dislocations. But not, at any rate, in the cases mentioned before. For just as, they say, those who claim to take beneficial things from indication do not say that all things indicate (for the Methodists say that some of the apparent things indicate, and not all, and the Rationalists [some] of the hidden things, and not all), so too the Empiricists say they make observation not upon all symptoms but upon some. For they do not think that all past things, nor all present ones, are useful for observation. For instance, someone has been bitten by a dog; the Empiricist, coming in, inquires only whether [it was] by a rabid one, and of the other antecedent things he examines not a single one; and likewise with present things: for [he observes] neither upon straightness of hair, as I said, nor upon curliness. fixed.before: Moreover, since our father is rich in speech and has learned through length of life to make what he says seem present, skilled at imposing compulsion on minds through the ear, he says that food is common to all who live in humanity, and he demands from one what no one may refuse, alleging in general that whatever the earth has produced is owed to all. fixed.before: But someone might raise a difficulty. If we remember with the same faculty with which we also perceive, there would be no memory of intelligibles. But there is such memory, for we remember theorems, and the intellect dwells on the more universal of these above all. If so, it remains to say that remembering belongs not to the perceptive soul alone but also to the rational soul. Or is it rather that memory is of perceptibles in itself, as imagination also is, but of intelligibles incidentally? For the intellect is interwoven with imagination, and from the impressions inscribed in imagination by actual perception it strips off the universals. Just as there is no imagination without actual perception, so there is no grasping of the universal apart from imagination. If this is so, it is clear what follows. Perception sees in itself the elephant painted at Athens, but incidentally the one grazing in India. Or again, when we see this Socrates here, we think besides of the common and specific human being. In the same way memory is active in itself about the impressions and residues in imagination, but incidentally about universals. So memory belongs in itself to the primary perceptive faculty, to which imagination also belongs, and incidentally to what is thought. For the same thing happens in thinking as in drawing a diagram. In drawing, we make no use of the triangle's being of a definite size, and yet we draw it definite in size. (In the demonstration that the three angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles, we need no definite size for the demonstration. Whether each of the sides is supposed a finger long, or a span long, or any length whatever, they will be shown to be equal to two right angles. fixed.work: De non parcendo in deum delinquentibus
fixed.author: Lucifer, Bishop of Cagliari
fixed.before: Since sacred Scripture reports that the blessed apostles acted thus, are we, the appointed overseers of God's churches, to keep silent while you invite the hearts of all to deny the Son of God and busy yourself with establishing your heresy, so that, evidently, we may not be found to have been insulting to you, a blasphemer, a murderer, a destroyer of God's religion? Sacred Scripture says that the apostles feared neither the blows nor the threats of the sons of pestilence, but always taught; were we to be broken by the force of your perishable reign, so that you could carry out all your wicked attempts? We are judged stubborn by you because true things are told you by us. So too your fellow-blasphemers condemned the most blessed Stephen, because he said to them: 'Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit; as your fathers [did], so do you. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced the coming of the Just One, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become, you who received the law by the ordering of angels and did not keep it.' When the Jews heard these things, were they rightly stirred against the most holy martyr Stephen, or wrongly? If wrongly, then see that you too are wrongly stirred against those who want you saved. Notice that you stand against the Church of God on that side on which the Jews stood then and are standing now; that you are thus stiff-necked, thus uncircumcised in heart and ears; that is why, just as they, hearing true things, did not endure them but rushed to kill a worshipper of God, you too are rushing to kill us who tell you things sound and plain. 'Now when they heard these things,' says divine Scripture, 'they raged in their hearts and gnashed their teeth at him'; and below: 'And crying out with a loud voice, they stopped their ears and rushed at him with one mind, and having cast him out of the city they stoned him.' So you, raging in heart and gnashing your teeth, are against us for no other reason than that we call you a persecutor of God's house, a destroyer of God's religion, a shedder of the blood of Christ's servants, that we rightly name you sacrilegious, since [you are] a blaspheming heretic, since [you are] one who assails the apostolic and evangelical faith. We do nothing hateful to God if, dealing with you in this manner, we tell you what we understand you to be. For we find that men such as you are acted thus against the glorious. 'And as they were ministering,' says Scripture, 'and fasting to the Lord, the Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them. Then, fasting and praying, they laid hands on them and sent them off. And they, sent out by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia and from there sailed to Cyprus. And when they had come to Salamis, they preached the word of the Lord in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John as assistant. And when they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they found a certain man, a Jewish false prophet, whose name was Bar-Jesus, which is interpreted "Ready", who was with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, a prudent man; he, having summoned Barnabas and Saul, sought to hear the word of God. But Elymas the magician (for so his name is said to be interpreted) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. But Saul, who is Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, fixing his eyes on him, said: O full of all deceit and fraud, son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness, you do not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord. And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is against you, and you will be blind, not seeing the sun for a time. And at once mist and darkness fell upon him, and going about he sought someone to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul, seeing what had happened, believed, amazed with wonder at the teaching of the Lord.' We believe that, instructed by this testimony, you will not say: 'Lucifer insults me, the emperor.'

For do I not regard you, the emperor Constantius, just as the glorious Paul and Barnabas regarded Bar-Jesus the Jew? For you are found to be opposed to the name of the Lord just as he was; you resist the truth as he resisted it; you do not want men to believe in the only Son of God, [but] in you, and he [wanted them to believe] in that Jewish false prophet, only because you are driven by a hostile spirit just as he was driven. For when you hear that the proconsul was a prudent man and desired to be instructed by the blessed apostles, so that he might grasp the way of truth, and that he whose imitator you are resisted the apostles, so that they should not lead the proconsul to believe in the Son of God, it is plain that you are such as that Jewish false prophet was. Likewise, since holy Scripture says that Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, uttered that invective, you ought to understand that that Jewish false prophet was full of an unclean spirit. So, just as he, driven by a hostile spirit, spoke against [them], since you too are found to resist in this way at the prompting of the Adversary, you must judge yourself to be none other than Bar-Jesus the Jewish false prophet. Therefore, since you understand that you are a second Bar-Jesus, a Jewish false prophet, as often as it has been said by your sacrilegious mouth, 'God has no true Son', do not take it ill if we say to you the things that were said by the apostle to your predecessor the Jewish false prophet: 'full of all deceit and fraud, son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness, who do not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord.' If you are stirred [to ask] why the things are said to you that were said to him whose road of death you are following, you will show yourself very foolish, wanting to be what that son, the Jewish false prophet, was, and not wanting to be called by the names by which he too was called. Again I both urge and beseech, as I also warn, that you be willing to take thought for yourself, so that eternal punishment may not receive you. For if he deserved to be blinded thus because he tried to resist, consider what evils can be set before you, a murderer, a sacrilegious man, a destroyer of God's religion, both in this life and for ever. Take further the things that can teach you that we are not insulting, but truthful. Those seven most glorious brothers resisted Antiochus, just as we now have resisted you. You have read what the fourth answered your fellow-pestilence, you who deign to keep crying out that I am insulting because I tell you that unless you are converted to God you will perish for ever; for he says: 'It is better, being given over to death by men, to await from God the hope of being raised again by him; for you there will be no resurrection to life.' fixed.work: De non parcendo in deum delinquentibus
fixed.author: Lucifer, Bishop of Cagliari
fixed.before: You are aggrieved that we reveal to those entrusted to us both you and who you are, and that it is fitting that you, the shadow of Antichrist, be trampled by all the soldiers of Christ. 'Who,' you say, 'have been able to trample me?' Those whom, because they confess themselves Christians, you keep shut up in prisons, deprive of their patrimony, drive into exile, torture, kill. Hence you judge us insolent, because we beseech all entrusted to us to trample the devil's head, to bring your sacrilegious attempts to nothing by the power of the sufferings inflicted on them for Christ, the only Son of God. Let that most glorious mother of these seven sons also be insolent in your eyes, because she deigned to entice her sons to conquer your fellow-madman Antiochus, saying: 'I do not know how you appeared in my womb, nor did I give you breath and life, nor did I myself put together the limbs of each of you; but the Creator of the world, who formed the birth of man and who searches out the origin of all things, will in his mercy give you back both breath and life, as you now disregard yourselves for the sake of his laws.' The devout mother did not cease to say these things to her sons, loving her sons bravely, until she saw them all killed. Were we, by contrast, whom he had foretold by the mouth of the prophet as the future shepherds of his flock, saying, 'And I will give you shepherds after my own heart, and they will feed you, feeding [you] with discipline', to keep silent, so that we might not seem insolent to you, a raging wolf coming to slaughter God's sheep? A woman so kindled her sons' hearts with the love of God that by their death she won the victories of the sword; and you have thought it fitting for us to say to Christ's soldiers: 'Do not take up arms against Constantius, the devil's henchman; do not resist the temple of all demons; rather, do whatever he commands to be done.' What is this stubbornness of ours, if we strive to fulfil the office delegated to us by God, if, in short, we are found to be imitators of that woman? You want to please the devil, whose work you are found to perform; you do not at all want us, by acting against you in these things, to become most acceptable to God. If it still moves you that you are called those things by us, take also what that seventh son of this woman cried out thus against Antiochus: 'But Antiochus, thinking himself scorned and despising the voice of her who reproached [him], while the youngest still survived, not only exhorted him with words but also affirmed with an oath that he would make him rich and happy, would transfer him from his ancestral ways, would have him as a friend, and would entrust him with affairs of state. But as the youth paid no heed to this, he called the mother and urged her to become [the means] of the youth's safety. And when he had exhorted her with many words, she undertook to persuade her son. So, bending towards him, she mocked the cruel tyrant and said in her ancestral tongue: Son, have pity on me, who carried you in my womb for ten months, and gave you milk for three years, and nourished you and brought you to this age. I beg you, child, look at heaven and earth, and having observed all that is in them, understand that God made them out of nothing, and that the human race comes to be thus, so that you may not fear this executioner, but, proving worthy of your brothers, may accept death, so that in that mercy he may receive you back with your brothers. When she had said this, the youth said: Whom are you waiting for? I do not obey the king's command, but I obey the precept of the law, which was given to us through Moses. But you, who have become the inventor of all malice against the Hebrews, will not escape the hand of God. For if, for the sake of rebuke and correction, our Lord is a little angry with us, yet he will be reconciled again to his servants. And you, O wicked man and most shameful of all men, do not vainly exalt yourself, puffed up with empty hopes against his servants; for you have not yet escaped the judgement of the almighty God who sees all things. For our brothers, having now endured brief pain, have fallen under God's covenant of eternal life; but you, by the judgement of God, will pay the just penalties of your pride. And I, like my brothers, give up both soul and body for our ancestral laws, calling on God to become merciful to our nation soon, and [to make] you confess with torments and blows that he alone is God. And in me and in my brothers the wrath of the Almighty will come to rest, which has justly been brought upon our whole nation.'

fixed.author: Maximus Taurinensis Episcopus
fixed.before: Every word of God, brothers, ought indeed to be heard with full attention and care of mind, but most of all this one, which we are going to address to your charity today. So you ought to hear what we say with reverence as much greater as these things, which are entrusted only to the baptized and to faithful hearers, are greater than those which even catechumens are accustomed to hear. You should not be surprised, dearest brothers, that during the mysteries themselves we said nothing to you about the mysteries, and that we did not at once interpret what we handed on. For we paid to things so holy and divine the honour of silence, and amid those sacred rites of the mysteries we refrain from the office of teaching, so that by keeping silent we may venerate the more the great majesty of divine grace, which no human voice can worthily unfold. But since it is necessary for your love to be instructed and taught in everything, now that the order of the mysteries has been completed, we set out for you the things we handed on before, lest, while you understand less of the dignity of the divine mystery, you should think it less precious. If you understand it, you will see that everything believed precious in this world is utterly worthless in comparison with so great a sacrament. Let each one of you, then, recall the several forms of the mysteries which, by the Lord's gift, you obtained through our ministry, and what you then received simply and faithfully, now understand with discernment, so that you may better keep what you have understood. First of all, certainly, we anointed your ears with the oil of blessing; but learn for what reason this is done, according to the tradition of the Church, by all the catholic priests of Christ. The entry of faith and of all holy doctrine is admitted to the soul through the ears, and understanding springs from hearing. For no one can come to know the sacraments of faith unless he hears someone preaching, as the blessed Apostle affirms, who says: But how will they hear without a preacher? and again: So faith [comes] from hearing, and hearing through the word of God (Rom. 10). Rightly, then, the organs of that sense are sanctified with that oil without which faith cannot reach the soul. At the same time [this is done] so that those coming to baptism may keep their ears unpolluted by every evil and shameful word to the very end, and, as if deaf, may not hear one who disparages his neighbour or one who speaks obscene and shameless things, fulfilling that saying of divine Scripture in which it is said: Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue (Sirach 28:28). And elsewhere: Do not believe an empty report. And again: Apply your heart to discipline, and make ready your ear for words of prudence (Prov. 23; Sirach). So the holy anointing applied to the ears signifies that they should turn away from and flee all words outside discipline, as [words] speaking against the teaching of Christ, and turn themselves to hearing the words of God alone, because, once the oil was smeared on, they have kept their hearing for the sayings of Christ. For the ears of Christ's faithful are truly perfected when they desire to hear nothing but Christ and the things that are Christ's. Hence in the Gospel the same Lord, when he was speaking of the mystery of the heavenly kingdom, said: He who has ears to hear, let him hear (Matt. 11, 13; Mark 4, and elsewhere). For though it is common to all to have ears, yet it is not common [to all] to have ears to hear. For whoever despise the words of God, although they cannot despise them unless they first hear them, yet because they despise what they hear, are not said to have heard either, since they disdain what they have heard as though unheard. Of hearers of this kind the Lord speaks in the Gospel: But blessed are your eyes, which see, and your ears, which hear (Matt. 13). And again: Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be likened to a wise man who built his house upon rock; and the rain came down, and the rivers came, and the winds blew and came against that house, and it did not fall, for it was founded upon firm rock (Matt. 7). You see, then, how great the difference is between one who hears well and one who hears badly: that is, between him who keeps the words of God and him who has heard them and despises them as though never heard. To the one who obeys and does, wisdom is ascribed; to this one who has despised, folly. The one builds on a solid foundation; this one's building is described as vain and, being without foundation, bound to fall easily. There is stability, here ruin, and great ruin. For no one falls more heavily than he who, having heard the word of God, turns to sins, for which eternal punishments have been prepared. This is understood to be done so that those who come to baptism may be admonished to keep the sacrament of so great a mystery inviolate and whole until death, so that, as long as they draw the breath of this life through their nostrils, they may not withdraw from the worship and service of Christ our Lord. Hence the holy man Job also says: As the Lord lives, who has taken away my judgement, and the Almighty, who has brought my soul to bitterness, as long as breath remains in me and the spirit of God in my nostrils, my lips will not speak iniquity, nor will my tongue speak a lie. For the scent of that oil, which has been blessed in the name and power of Christ, calls you to a spiritual sense of smell, so that you may perceive Christ with inestimable sweetness, not with the senses of the body but of the mind; and, delighted by knowledge of his fragrance, following in his footsteps, you may be able to say what the choir of believers says to God: We run after you toward the scent of your ointments (Song 1). This we desire to be fulfilled in you also, dearly beloved brothers: that when you yourselves have received the good fragrance of the knowledge of Christ, a most sweet fragrance may rise up to God from the holiness of your life as well. Through [our] Lord, etc.

objection.english: was born with less than an eye
objection.explain: This means 'was born lacking an eye', not with less than a whole eye.

fixed.before: But those [whose parts are] smaller [are like someone] who, as if some necessary part had been naturally taken away, was born with less than an eye, or cut short in some other limb, and so received a natural loss of the fullness of his whole. Between these, however, as between equal excesses, that number which is called perfect has obtained the moderation of the middle limit, an imitator of virtue, which is neither carried on by a superfluous advance nor, again, drawn back by a cramped diminution, but holds the mean; it neither runs riot with abundance in its equal parts nor lacks through poverty, as 6 or 28. For six has a half, that is 3, and a third, that is 2, and a sixth, that is 1, which, if they are brought into one sum, that is 3, 2, 1, the whole body of the number is found equal to its parts. And 28 has a half, 14, and a quarter, 7, and a seventh, 4, and a fourteenth, 2, [and] a twenty-eighth, 1, which, brought together, will equal the whole body with its parts; for the parts joined in one make 28. There is also in these a great likeness of virtue and vice: for you will find perfect numbers rarely, and they are easily counted, since they are few and produced in a very constant order. But superabundant ones you will find without limit, arranged in no orders, here and there and without order, and generated from no fixed end. For first [comes] 6, then 28, after these 416, [ending in] the same six as the first; after that 800 and 128, [ending in] the same eight as the second.

objection.english: unity is preceded by two by a unit
objection.explain: Here 'praeceditur' means 'is exceeded': two exceeds one by one, rather than preceding it in numerical order.

fixed.before: But if anyone seeks superparticulars in this table, he will find them in this way. If he marks the second angle, whose beginning is four, and over which lies two, and fits the following row to it, the sesquialter proportion is shown. For the third [row] is sesquialter of the second, as three to two, or six to 4, or nine to six, or 12 to 8; and likewise, if such a pairing is made in the other numbers in the same series, no unlikeness of variation will slip in; yet the same exceeding of the sums is here too as was in the doubles. For the first exceeds the first, that is three [exceeds] two, by one, the second the second by two, the third the third by three, and so on. But if the fourth row is compared with the third, as 4 to 3, and you follow the rest in the same order, a sesquitertian comparison is gathered, as 4 to 3, or 8 to 6, or 12 to 9: do you see how in all these the sesquitertian is kept? Moreover, if, doing the same, you compare those beneath them with the following rows of the other, you will recognise all the superparticular species without any hindrance. And this is divine in this arrangement, that all the angular numbers are square. A square, to put it most briefly (it will also be explained more broadly), is called that which two equal numbers multiply, as is the case in this table too: for one once is one, and it is a square in potency. Likewise twice two are 4, three times three 9, which multiplications into themselves have made from their first elements. objection.english: For the majesty of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is never separated from [their] omnipotence.

And since the person of the one sent is one, that of the sender another, that of the one promising another, both unity and Trinity are shown to us together; so that the essence, having equality and not admitting solitude, is understood to be both of the same substance and not of the same person. For if man, made in the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1), had remained in the honour of his nature, and had not, deceived by the devil's fraud, strayed through concupiscence from the law laid down for him, the creator of the world would not have become a creature: nor would the eternal have undergone temporality, or God the Son, equal to God the Father, have taken the form of a servant and the likeness of sinful flesh. objection.original: cujus cum sit naturaliter invisibilis pulchritudo, visibilis fiet peccatorum sorde deformitas
objection.english: whose beauty, though it is by nature invisible, will become a visible deformity through the filth of sins
objection.explain: The soul's ugliness from sin will become visible; its beauty is not said to turn into ugliness.

fixed.author: Ambrose, Saint, Bishop of Milan
fixed.before: CHAPTER XXIX.—I want you to tell me what is the glory of present things, what are the fruits of this time, what the use of perishable things. The power of a kingdom, as I have said, is ended by death; the ambition of authority is cut off by succession; abundance of riches is often withdrawn from us while we live; the enjoyment of pleasure is spoiled when sadness intervenes; the delight of joys is violated by the dread of fear; and everything that is seized by desire, whatever the body or the soul of the body desires, is cut down by the sickle of the end. Nor can anything obtain the perfect privilege of blessedness which the infinity of eternity does not surround; for that must be perishable which is measured by inevitable necessity: that whose life a chance event sometimes cuts off will without doubt remain liable, inconstant and weak. Since all these things, then, are ended by death, what is our own in death itself? If we have nothing by which conscience is burdened with the increase of good work; and if we have been able to have nothing good of our own, what shall we carry with us as we return to our homeland? How naked and misshapen will our soul remain, if we do not at least cover it with the veils of penance and the garments of confession! unless it be that we hasten to hide our disgrace, and do not strive to cover the nakedness of the soul; whose beauty, though it is by nature invisible, will become a visible deformity through the filth of sins.

objection.original: καὶ πάντας γλαυ- κοειδεῖς τὴν ἰδέαν αὐτῶν
objection.english: and all of them grey-eyed in appearance
objection.explain: The fleas should be grey-blue in appearance, without specifying eye colour; the same over-specification occurs in the teacher's proposal.

fixed.author: Syntipas
fixed.before: And after changing his appearance he stood very close to that old man, and first he saw come to him the man who had bought his aromatic woods. He reported to that teacher, saying: 'I met a merchant bringing some aromatic woods for sale, and bought up his whole cargo, giving him what I agreed, namely a dish filled with whatever goods he might see fit to ask of me.' The teacher answered him, saying: 'And what is it you agreed to give him? Gold? Silver?' The trickster says: 'No, my lord; none of these, but unnamed kinds [of goods], whatever he himself might want, a full dish.' The teacher said to him: 'You have made a great mistake. For if the merchant happened to ask you for fleas, a full dish, half of them to be female and the other half male, and moreover to be grey-eyed, would you have been able to give him such a payment? How could you have escaped him?' The trickster says to him: 'This merchant, my lord, is not so clever, nor was his mind capable of such craftiness. But, as I think, he is going to ask me for either gold or silver.' Then the one who had beaten the merchant in debate came forward too and reported, saying: 'I too contended with the merchant in conversation and the weaving of arguments, and having defeated him I ordered him to drink all the waters of the sea. For so it had been agreed between us, that the one beaten in argument should accept and do whatever was ordered by the winner.' The teacher answered him: 'Neither have you acted well. For suppose perhaps he were to reply to you: "Go first and hold back the rivers that flow into the sea; then in this way I will drink the water of the sea, which alone I agreed with you to drink." If then he says this to you, will you easily be able to check the rivers from flowing into the sea?' The trickster says: 'But know that the merchant's sense is not sufficient to make such a reply to me.' Then the one-eyed trickster too came forward and said to the old man: 'I too, my lord, saw in the market a foreign merchant who was grey in the eyes. And seizing him I said to him: "You and I are both grey-[eyed], and you have stolen one of my eyes. So I will by no means let go of you until I take out one of your eyes and fasten it to my forehead, or you redeem [it] with your whole property."' The teacher said: 'Neither have you achieved anything. For if he sees fit to reply to you: "First, to establish this claim of yours, take out this one eye which you have, and I likewise will put out one of my eyes, and let us both weigh them; and if they are found equal in weight to each other, it is clear that my one eye is yours; but if one of the two eyes being weighed appears heavier than the other in the pan of the scale, then my other eye is not yours, but rather you will be duly called to account for putting it out." If then the merchant answers you this, will he not entirely dissuade you from your claim? And the worst of it is that if this happens to you, you will be completely deprived of sight and become entirely eyeless, whereas he, still having one of his eyes afterwards, will go on seeing the light.' To this the one-eyed trickster replies to the teacher: 'But this merchant is not so crafty as to put forward against me such a plausible defence.' While these things were thus being said and answered back between the tricksters and their teacher, the merchant listened very well and secretly through that whole night and kept these things in his own heart. When morning came the man who had bought the aromatic woods comes to the merchant. And the merchant says: 'Give me, friend, whatever you agreed to provide me in return for the cargo sold to you.' The trickster said to him: 'Ask whatever you want, and I will readily provide it to you.' The merchant [said]: 'I want you to give me in the dish as many fleas as it will hold, half of the swarm male and the other half female, and all of them grey-eyed in appearance.' Having said this to the trickster, the merchant kept pressing him hard and using much force against him, until the trickster, even against his will, gave him an amount greater than the fair price of his aromatic woods; and so he was rid of his harassment. Meeting also the other two tricksters, the one contending about the eye and the one who had ordered him to drink up the sea, he demanded that they too do what he had secretly heard from their teacher. And he kept throttling them too, until the merchant received from them as many gifts as he wanted (to be persuaded); and so they were rid of his harassment. And now, my lord king, from what I have told you know that both those two children, the three-year-old and the five-year-old, of whom I told you before, and this aged teacher, were adorned with much knowledge and understanding; and like them my teacher too has made me a teacher."

objection.english: O God, have mercy for Martin's sake
objection.explain: Martini is the genitive object of miserere: 'O God, have mercy on Martin,' not 'for Martin's sake.'

not_upheld.reason: Martini goes with deus: 'God of Martin, have mercy'. The sailors pray for themselves (miseros, line 2), not for Martin, a saint already in glory. 'Have mercy for Martin's sake' gives that sense loosely; Codex's 'have mercy on Martin' does not.

objection.original: Qui cito traiciet Gothis inrumpentibus amne.
objection.english: he who will soon cross the river with the Goths bursting in.
objection.explain: Qui refers to ense, the sword that will soon pierce; the Goths burst across the river in the ablative absolute, rather than an unnamed man crossing it.

not_upheld.reason: qui more naturally takes up the subject who knocks and girds himself with the sword, and traiciet 'will cross over' fits the Goths breaking in by the river (amne); editors who print amnem read it so. Codex's reading, the sword that will pierce, is possible but not required.

not_upheld.reason: 'Exceed the measure of fairness' is a fair rendering of mensuram aequitatis; 'moderation' is a matter of preference.

objection.explain: Temporal origin, spatial movement and growth are the subjects of est: each constitutes a limit for creatures, rather than being listed alongside a separately asserted end.
